clue.text: Sharp decline of a soak

blocks.note: first meaning: a precipitous slope, the noun use of an adjective for sheer ground
second meaning: a period of soaking something in liquid, as tea or washing is left to sit

explanation.surface: A drunkard's sharp fall from grace.
explanation.walkthrough: A soak is slang for a heavy drinker, so the surface reads as a drunk's downfall; here it means a spell of soaking.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun the word names a sheer slope, and it also names the act of leaving something immersed in liquid.

clue.text: Ill-clad layabout type

blocks.note: surface reading: a scruffy idler who dresses badly
setter's reading: missing a key garment, the kind of person lazing about bare-chested in the sun

explanation.surface: A badly dressed loafer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone lounging about without the usual upper garment is literally poorly covered, which is what the adjective describes.

clue.text: Some self-interest is proper to fairyland

indicators.note: 'Some' means only part of the following phrase is taken, a run of letters lying inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the hyphen inside the phrase

explanation.surface: A remark that selfishness belongs only in fairy stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes things belonging to elves, the small magical folk of fairy tales.

clue.text: What a blow it was for mail deliveries

definitions.text: What a blow it was for mail deliveries

blocks.clueFragment: What a blow it was for mail deliveries
blocks.note: surface reading: some setback that hit the postal service
setter's reading: an instrument blown, sounded by the guard of a mail coach to announce its arrival

explanation.surface: A lament about a disaster for the postal service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' looks like a misfortune; it is something you blow into.
explanation.definitionFit: Mail coaches carried a long brass horn that the guard sounded to clear the road and signal arrivals.

clue.text: School of whiting over-takers ?

blocks.note: surface reading: a group of fish that overtake whiting
setter's reading: in Alice in Wonderland a whiting complains of the sea creature close behind it treading on its tail

explanation.surface: A school of sea creatures racing past the whiting.
explanation.walkthrough: The Lobster Quadrille in Alice in Wonderland has a whiting tell a snail to hurry, with one close behind treading on its tail.
explanation.definitionFit: These marine mammals travel in schools, and Lewis Carroll's song has one about to overtake a whiting.

clue.text: Stay in short to make the pace or the scene

linkWords: in short to make the pace or

blocks.note: first meaning: a support or strut
second meaning: short for property, an object used to dress a stage set; the clue also hints at a propeller, which makes an aircraft's pace

explanation.surface: Advice to a pacemaker on staying in short to set the speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' says the word is an abbreviation: of propeller, which makes the pace, or of property, which makes the scene.
explanation.definitionFit: A support is a stay, and theatre slang shortens property, any movable object on stage, to the same four letters.

clue.text: Petal-thin panes?

blocks.note: surface reading: very delicate glass
setter's reading: glass arranged like the petals of a flower around a centre

explanation.surface: Glazing so fine it is as thin as petals.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular church window has tracery radiating like petals of a flower, each segment glazed.

clue.text: Gold snaffles for heavenly roundabouts

blocks.note: or is the heraldic word for gold
a snaffle is a simple kind of horse's bit

explanation.surface: Gold being grabbed in exchange for fairground rides.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Snaffles' looks like a verb meaning grabs; it is the plural noun for a horse's mouthpiece.
explanation.definitionFit: Planets and moons travel in circular paths around another body, the celestial equivalent of going round and round.

clue.text: Take the fork to the Junction

definitions.text: Take the fork to the Junction

blocks.clueFragment: Take the fork to the Junction
blocks.note: surface reading: driving directions, bear off at the fork to reach the junction
setter's reading: what you eat with a fork, which also names a famous tangled road interchange

explanation.surface: Road directions telling a driver which fork leads to the junction.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gravelly Hill Interchange in Birmingham, opened in 1972, is nicknamed after a tangled plate of pasta.
explanation.definitionFit: The long pasta is eaten by twirling it on a fork, and lends its name to Birmingham's knotted motorway junction.

clue.text: Motes detected with, their aid?

blocks.note: surface reading: tiny particles of dust that need help to be spotted
setter's reading: motes are specks, and the tool for seeing specks is a near namesake

explanation.surface: Dust particles that can only be spotted with some help.
explanation.walkthrough: Motes are specks of dust, and the answer is the informal word for glasses, which sound almost the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Spectacles, informally shortened, are the optical aid that lets weak eyes pick out tiny particles.

clue.text: Char leaves in hot water? If so U.S. inn suffers

indicators.note: something that suffers is knocked about, so the letters before it are battered into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the stops
taken as written

explanation.surface: An American hotel suffers if its tea is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Char is British slang for tea, and 'in hot water' doubles as being in trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea leaves steeped in hot water make brews of the kind called by this name, liquids extracting flavour.

clue.text: One or two of those Blake damned

definitions.text: One or two of those Blake damned

blocks.clueFragment: One or two of those Blake damned
blocks.note: surface reading: a handful of the people the poet condemned
setter's reading: one strap of a pair of trouser supports, or a pair itself

explanation.surface: A few of the sinners William Blake condemned.
explanation.walkthrough: Blake's Proverbs of Hell say 'Damn braces: Bless relaxes'. The singular word is one of those supports, and also means a pair.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a pair of game birds and also the singular of the straps that hold trousers up.

clue.text: Hot under canvas for those right beside Dot

indicators.note: to be under canvas is to be inside a shelter, so one letter sits within the other word

blocks.note: canvas stands for the shelters made of it, as in sleeping under canvas
H is the abbreviation for hot on taps

explanation.surface: Campers who are too hot in their tents next to someone called Dot.
explanation.walkthrough: Dot looks like a name; it is the decimal point.
explanation.definitionFit: In decimal notation the first digit after the point counts parts of ten, so those places sit immediately right of it.

clue.text: Administers corporal pun- punishment on and off

definitions.note: the scan repeats pun- across a line break; read it as punishment

blocks.note: first meaning: beats with a thin flexible cane
second meaning: the devices that turn a light or machine on and off

explanation.surface: Someone who canes others only intermittently.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed 'pun- punishment' is a scanning slip for punishment. 'On and off' reads as 'now and then'; it is the two settings of a toggle.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means thrashes with a slender stick, and as a plural noun the controls that toggle power.

clue.text: Mab, I levant from this love-hate sort of relationship

definitions.note: a noun phrase for an adjective: the answer describes such a relationship

indicators.note: the answer is said to come out of the preceding words, so they are rearranged to make it

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Queen Mab announcing she is running off from a stormy love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: Mab is the fairy queen, and to levant is an old word for absconding, which makes the surface a flight from a lover.
explanation.definitionFit: Holding mixed, contradictory feelings toward someone, loving and loathing together, is exactly this two-sided state.

clue.text: Unusual mine: get one who knows to come round to test

indicators.note: something unusual is out of its normal form, so the letters of the next word are reordered
coming round something means surrounding it, so one part wraps the other

blocks.note: a specialist is someone with deep knowledge
the letters of mine, reordered

explanation.surface: An odd-looking mine needs a specialist to come and examine it.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial carried out to find something out, or the act of trying, is the same as a test.

clue.text: Bunthorne with alternative to poppy or lily

definitions.text: Bunthorne with alternative to poppy or lily

blocks.note: Reginald Bunthorne is the posturing aesthetic bard in Gilbert and Sullivan's Patience
another flower that could be carried instead

explanation.surface: Gilbert and Sullivan's aesthete carrying a different flower.
explanation.walkthrough: In Patience Bunthorne sings of walking down Piccadilly 'with a poppy or a lily in your medieval hand'; he is also a sham versifier, so the whole clue defines.
explanation.definitionFit: Bunthorne is a fraud whose verses are worthless, the very type of an inferior rhymester.

clue.text: What's to show for your fag, feller ?

definitions.text: What's to show for your fag, feller ?

blocks.clueFragment: What's to show for your fag, feller
blocks.note: surface reading: a question to a chap about what his cigarette has got him
setter's reading: one who fells trees, left with the stump, as a smoker is left with a cigarette end

explanation.surface: Someone asking a smoker what good his cigarette did him.
explanation.walkthrough: A fag is British slang for a cigarette, and 'feller' is both a chap and someone who cuts down trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The short butt left after smoking, or the stump left after cutting a tree, is the remaining end of either.

clue.text: Diehards fight to the last pint

definitions.text: Diehards fight to the last pint

blocks.clueFragment: Diehards fight to the last pint
blocks.note: surface reading: stubborn drinkers holding out until the final glass
setter's reading: the final dregs of a pint of the British hoppy ale, which is also the idiom for the very finish

explanation.surface: Stubborn pub regulars holding out until the final round.
explanation.walkthrough: Bitter is a British pint of hoppy ale, so its last part names the phrase diehards fight to.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom for the final, hardest stage of a struggle is what stubborn people say they will fight until.

clue.text: Of certain singular-looking people

blocks.note: surface reading: describing people of odd appearance
setter's reading: looking with a single eye, like the giants of Greek myth

explanation.surface: A description of some strange-looking folk.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to the one-eyed giants of Greek legend, whose single eye makes their gaze literally solitary.

clue.text: So much for bishops, Janus observes

indicators.note: Janus is the two-faced Roman god looking both ways, so the word reads the same forwards and backwards

blocks.note: first meaning: the dioceses, the seats of episcopal authority
second meaning: notices, looks at

explanation.surface: Janus watching, and dismissing the bishops.
explanation.definitionFit: A bishop's diocese is his seat or territory, and the plural noun doubles as the verb for looking at.

clue.text: He's upset (or is he?) to say " Tiny miss, go "

definitions.text: He's upset (or is he?) to say " Tiny miss, go "

indicators.note: something upset is overturned and disordered, so the quoted letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man, apparently troubled, telling a little girl to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue is a man who dismisses a young woman, and '(or is he?)' teases whether he is distressed or pleased.
explanation.definitionFit: A man who dislikes women would gladly send a girl away, which is what the whole clue pictures.

clue.text: Great man with phoney, groovy reputation

definitions.text: Great man with phoney, groovy reputation

blocks.clueFragment: Great man with phoney, groovy reputation
blocks.note: surface reading: a celebrity whose fame is fake but fashionable
setter's reading: the phonograph, which played sound recorded in grooves

explanation.surface: A celebrated figure whose trendy fame is a sham.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Phoney' looks like fake; it stands for the phonograph, and 'groovy' points to its grooved cylinders.
explanation.definitionFit: The American inventor Thomas Alva made his name with the phonograph, which recorded sound in grooves.

clue.text: Up, man (you've lost a stack), play what's dealt

blocks.note: to be up is to be standing
Pat is a common man's name

explanation.surface: A poker player told to get up after losing his chips, and to play the hand he holds.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracket is surface colour: a pile of chips is a stack, and the order 'Up, Pat' fits a fallen loser.
explanation.definitionFit: In poker, refusing to draw new cards and keeping the hand dealt is the idiom for holding firm.

clue.text: Alcoholic leaves ?

blocks.note: surface reading: a drunk walks out
setter's reading: a name for a drink of fruit juice and rum, shared with a leafy garden plant

explanation.surface: A drunk walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: Shrub is an old punch of spirits, sugar and fruit, and the same word is a woody plant with foliage.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a sweetened rum cordial and a bushy plant covered in foliage.

clue.text: Is able to confound Pascal

indicators.note: confounding means throwing into confusion, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone clever enough to baffle a great mathematician.
explanation.walkthrough: Pascal looks like a surname to outwit; the answer is his first name.
explanation.definitionFit: The French mathematician and philosopher Pascal had this forename, so it is an example of what he was called.

clue.text: Arragon's blinking portrait

blocks.note: surface reading: an annoying picture belonging to a prince
setter's reading: in The Merchant of Venice the silver casket holds the portrait of a blinking fool

explanation.surface: A prince exasperated with his own painted likeness.
explanation.walkthrough: The Prince of Arragon chooses silver and finds 'the portrait of a blinking idiot'; 'blinking' is a mild British curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's suitor finds a picture of a fool, his reward for choosing wrongly, which mocks him as one.

clue.text: Down town

definitions.note: a verb: to put down into the ground

blocks.note: first meaning: to put down into the earth, inter
second meaning: a town in Greater Manchester, England

explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to put underground, and a Lancashire mill town near Manchester bears the same name.

clue.text: The ceremonies don't sound sinister

indicators.note: sound tells us the word is heard rather than read, so spelling may differ

blocks.note: turns the following word into its opposite, so the side meant is the other one
sinister is Latin for left, and things that are not on the left are on the other hand

explanation.surface: Rituals that don't seem menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sinister' looks like menacing; it is the heraldic left, and 'don't' turns it into its opposite.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal religious or solemn ceremonies are the same thing as rituals, plural like the definition.

clue.text: Instanced by Tweedle-dum. --dee on a seesaw ?

definitions.text: Instanced by Tweedle-dum. --dee on a seesaw ?

blocks.clueFragment: Instanced by Tweedle-dum. --dee on a seesaw
blocks.note: surface reading: the twin brothers playing on a seesaw
setter's reading: two identical twins weigh the same, so the plank stays level

explanation.surface: Carroll's identical twins playing on a seesaw.
explanation.walkthrough: Tweedledum and Tweedledee in Through the Looking-Glass are indistinguishable, so on a seesaw neither end would sink.
explanation.definitionFit: Perfect balance between equal weights is what a level plank with matching twins shows.

clue.text: Rank of  the  bartender's victim

blocks.note: surface reading: the status of someone a barman has wronged
setter's reading: a Bart-ender, something that ends a Bart, the abbreviation used after a hereditary knight's name

explanation.surface: The social standing of someone a barman has done for.
explanation.walkthrough: Bart. is the abbreviation written after a baronet's name, so a Bart-ender finishes off the title itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A hereditary title ranking below a baron is ended when the last holder dies without an heir.

clue.text: Summoned to court-said to have been seen

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the next phrase is heard rather than spelt

blocks.note: spotted, glimpsed

explanation.surface: A witness called to court because he claims to have been seen.
explanation.definitionFit: A person ordered to appear before a judge has been formally named in a summons, which is the legal sense.
